title: Common R&D tax credit scams to avoid
description: R&D tax credit scams include inflating qualified expenses, relabeling routine work as research, fabricating projects and 10% to 30% contingency fees.
summary: Common R&D tax credit scams in the United States include inflating qualified research expenses with sales, marketing, and administrative wages, relabeling routine operations as research, fabricating projects, and charging 10% to 30% contingency fees. Because the claiming business remains legally liable, disallowed credits bring repayment, interest, penalties of 20% to 75%, and possible Form 8886 non-disclosure penalties.

body.text: Common R&D tax credit scams in the United States include inflating qualified research expenses with sales, marketing, and administrative wages, relabeling routine operations as research, fabricating projects, and charging 10% to 30% contingency fees. Because the claiming business remains legally liable, disallowed credits bring repayment, interest, penalties of 20% to 75%, and possible Form 8886 non-disclosure penalties.

Research and Development (R&D) tax credit scams operate primarily through two interconnected mechanisms: the systematic inflation of Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) by misclassifying routine business costs or non-technical wages, and the use of conflicted contingency fee arrangements ("no win, no fee" commissions typically ranging from 10% to 30% of the claimed benefit) that financially reward promoters for maximizing claim size regardless of statutory eligibility. Predatory consultants capture immediate percentage-based fees by promising to double or triple tax relief, often on the assumption that low audit rates will shield exaggerated filings, yet the claiming company retains non-delegable legal responsibility for the accuracy of its own tax return. When tax authorities disallow unsubstantiated claims, whether the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) in the United States or, in the comparative jurisdictions, HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) in the United Kingdom or the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) and the Department of Industry, Science and Resources (DISR, which administers the program through AusIndustry and was known as the Department of Industry, Science, Energy and Resources, or DISER, until it was renamed on July 1, 2022), the corporate taxpayer bears the full clawback of the credit alongside statutory penalties and interest.

items: Reportable Transaction Non-Disclosure Penalty Caps (26 U.S.C. § 6707A): While the overall statutory range under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 6707A spans from $5,000 to $200,000, the $200,000 maximum applies only to Listed Transactions under 26 U.S.C. § 6707A(b)(2)(A). Unless the underlying R&D scheme has been specifically designated by the IRS as a Listed Transaction, a contingent or refundable fee agreement constitutes a non-listed Transaction with Contractual Protection under 26 CFR § 1.6011-4(b)(4). For that category, the non-disclosure penalty equals 75% of the decrease in tax shown on the return as a result of the transaction, subject to a statutory minimum of $10,000 ($5,000 for natural persons) and a maximum of $50,000 for corporate and other entity taxpayers ($10,000 for natural persons) per failure under 26 U.S.C. § 6707A(b)(1)–(3). There is still no general "reasonable cause" defense, and rescission is discretionary and unavailable for Listed Transactions.

Jurisdictional Separation of Substantive Tax Penalties (UK 100% Cap vs. US Civil Penalty Tiers): The 100% penalty ceiling is a United Kingdom rule under Schedule 24 to the Finance Act 2007, where HMRC assesses up to 100% of "Potential Lost Revenue" (PLR) for deliberate and concealed inaccuracies and may, under Paragraph 19, require company officers to pay up to 100% of a penalty attributable to their deliberate inaccuracy. In the United States, substantive civil penalties on disallowed or fraudulent R&D credit claims follow a distinct statutory hierarchy: a 20% penalty for erroneous refund or credit claims made for an excessive amount without reasonable cause (26 U.S.C. § 6676(a)) or for accuracy-related underpayments (26 U.S.C. § 6662(a)); a 20% to 30% penalty for reportable transaction understatements (26 U.S.C. § 6662A(a), (c)); a 40% penalty for gross valuation misstatements or nondisclosed noneconomic substance transactions (26 U.S.C. § 6662(h)–(i)); and a 75% civil fraud penalty on underpayments attributable to fraud (26 U.S.C. § 6663(a)). These US penalties are coordinated rather than cumulative on the same dollars, a point explained in the worked example below.

ISO Standards Claims and Fee Structure Nuances: ISO 31000 (Risk Management) is a guidelines standard that the International Organization for Standardization states is not intended for certification, and its 2009 edition was replaced by ISO 31000:2018. A fee that depends on the taxpayer realizing a tax benefit falls squarely within the contingent-fee concept of 26 CFR § 1.6011-4(b)(4) for reportable transaction purposes, so any such engagement letter requires careful structuring and, where the condition applies to a federal income tax benefit, Form 8886 analysis.

Circular 230 Contingent Fee Rules After Ridgely v. Lew: In Ridgely v. Lew, No. 1:12-cv-00565 (D.D.C. July 16, 2014), the court, following Loving v. IRS, 742 F.3d 1013 (D.C. Cir. 2014), held that the IRS lacks statutory authority to promulgate or enforce the § 10.27 contingent-fee restrictions with respect to the preparation and filing of "ordinary refund claims" (refund claims filed before an examination begins), and enjoined enforcement to that extent. Because many R&D credit claims are filed as amended returns or refund claims, Circular 230 alone does not prevent a practitioner from pricing those claims on contingency. In December 2024, Treasury and the IRS proposed regulations (REG-116610-20) that would remove § 10.27 altogether. Independent constraints remain: state accountancy rules and the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct (ET § 1.510) prohibit CPAs from preparing original or amended returns or refund claims for a contingent fee, subject to narrow exceptions, and the reportable transaction rules under 26 CFR § 1.6011-4(b)(4) apply to the taxpayer regardless of the advisor's licensing status.

Revenue Procedure 2007-20 and Case-Law References: The revenue procedure in fact lists eight: the work opportunity credit (§ 51), the welfare-to-work credit (§ 51A), the Indian employment credit (§ 45A(a)), the low-income housing credit (§ 42(a)), the new markets tax credit (§ 45D(a)), the empowerment zone employment credit (§ 1396(a)), the renewal community employment credit (§ 1400H), and the Hurricane Katrina-era employee retention credit (§ 1400R(a), (b), or (c)). The research credit under § 41 is not on the list.

body.text: The Structural Anatomy of R&D Tax Credit Scams: Operational and Legal Deficiencies

Predatory R&D tax credit schemes exploit the technical intersection between engineering documentation and tax accounting. These schemes rely on two primary operational mechanisms: artificially expanding the base of Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) by sweeping in statutorily excluded wages and routine operational costs, and deploying high-pressure, non-transparent marketing practices that transfer severe audit and penalty exposure onto the claiming business. Both mechanisms depend on the claiming company not understanding the narrow statutory definitions that govern what may be claimed, which is why a precise grasp of those definitions is the most effective defense against a scam.
Systematic Inflation of Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) and Ineligible Wages

In the United States, the Credit for Increasing Research Activities is governed by 26 U.S.C. § 41 (Internal Revenue Code Section 41, made permanent by the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes [PATH] Act of 2015) and its implementing Treasury Regulations at 26 CFR §§ 1.41-1 through 1.41-9. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1)–(3) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2, a taxpayer's QREs are limited to the sum of "in-house research expenses" and "contract research expenses" paid or incurred in carrying on a trade or business. Contract research expenses are generally 65% of amounts paid to non-employees for qualified research performed on the taxpayer's behalf, where the taxpayer bears the expense regardless of the research's success and retains substantial rights in the results; the percentage rises to 75% for amounts paid to qualified research consortia and to 100% for amounts paid for qualified energy research to eligible small businesses, universities, and federal laboratories under § 41(b)(3)(D). In-house research expenses consist solely of (i) wages, as defined for income tax withholding purposes in 26 U.S.C. § 3401(a) (in practice, the amounts reported in Form W-2 Box 1), paid or incurred to an employee for "qualified services" performed by that employee; (ii) supplies, meaning tangible property other than land, improvements to land, and property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation, used in the conduct of qualified research; and (iii) amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research, which the regulations and IRS practice extend to qualifying off-premises computing and cloud-hosting arrangements under prescribed conditions.

Because employee compensation typically represents the largest component of an R&D claim, aggressive vendors systematically target wage allocations to inflate the credit base. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(1)–(3), employee wages qualify as QREs only to the extent the employee performs one of three narrowly defined categories of qualified services:

items: Engaging in qualified research (26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(1)): The actual, hands-on conduct of qualified research, such as a scientist or engineer conducting laboratory experiments or developing experimental prototypes.

Direct supervision of qualified research (26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2)): The immediate, first-line management of employees engaging in qualified research, such as a research scientist who directly supervises laboratory experiments without personally performing them. The regulation expressly excludes supervision by higher-level managers to whom first-line supervisors report, even if those managers are themselves qualified research scientists.

Direct support of qualified research (26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3)): Services in the direct support of persons either engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research or directly supervising such persons. Regulatory examples of eligible direct support include a machinist machining a part for an experimental model, a laboratory worker cleaning equipment used in qualified research, a clerk compiling research test data, and a secretary typing reports describing laboratory results derived from qualified research.

body.text: As documented by tax controversy practitioners at TaxOps and consistent with the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) on IRC § 41 Qualified Research Expenses, aggressive promoters routinely violate these boundaries through three specific wage-inflation practices. First, promoters include disqualified sales and marketing personnel. Although 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(D) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5) exclude efficiency surveys, management functions or techniques, and "market research, testing, or development (including advertising or promotions)" from qualified research, aggressive vendors claim 100% of sales and marketing employees' wages by rebranding their roles under labels such as "technical sales" or "market research." A salesperson who relays customer feedback to engineers is not engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting the experimental work itself, and the label on a job description does not change the statutory analysis.

Second, promoters sweep in general and administrative (G&A) and accounting staff. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) and the IRS ATG, direct support does not include general administrative services or other services that only indirectly benefit research activities, regardless of whether those administrative personnel sit in a separate department or are embedded within the research department. The regulations specifically state that the services of payroll personnel preparing salary checks for laboratory scientists, an accountant accounting for research expenses, a janitor performing general cleaning of a research laboratory, and officers engaged in supervising financial or personnel matters do not qualify as direct support.

Third, predatory vendors abuse the "substantially all" (80%) wage rule through blanket inclusion. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1)–(2), when an employee performs both qualified and nonqualified services during the taxable year, only the portion of wages allocable to qualified services constitutes an in-house research expense, unless at least 80 percent ("substantially all") of the employee's wages for the taxable year are paid for qualified services, in which case 100% of that employee's wages are treated as paid for qualified services. Aggressive consultants frequently claim 100% of wages for partial-support roles (such as testers or solutions engineers) without performing employee interviews, time-tracking analyses, or project-nexus substantiation. Tax Court decisions have repeatedly rejected wage allocations of this kind for senior personnel whose involvement was not substantiated; in Shami v. Commissioner, 741 F.3d 560 (5th Cir. 2014), for example, the court affirmed the disallowance of most of the wages claimed for two executives because the taxpayer could not prove what portion of their time was spent on qualified services.
Mischaracterization of Routine Operations and Fabrication of Claims

Beyond wage misclassification, predatory R&D schemes systematically mischaracterize routine commercial activities as eligible experimentation or fabricate research projects outright. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a) (applicable to taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003), research related to developing or improving a business component (defined in § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business) constitutes "qualified research" only if it satisfies every prong of the statutory Four-Part Test, applied separately to each business component:

items: Section 174 / 174A Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)): The expenditures must be eligible for treatment as research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174, or, following the 2025 budget reconciliation legislation (Pub. L. 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025), as domestic research or experimental expenditures under new IRC § 174A.

Technological in Nature Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4)): The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, meaning the process of experimentation fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.

Elimination of Uncertainty and Permitted Purpose Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and (d)(3); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3) and (a)(5)): The research must be intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of that component, for a qualified purpose: a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality. Research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors is excluded under § 41(d)(3)(B).

Process of Experimentation Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6)): Substantially all of the research activities with respect to the business component, defined in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) as 80 percent or more measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, must constitute elements of a process of experimentation designed to evaluate one or more alternatives (via modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error) to resolve the uncertainty.

body.text: The process-of-experimentation requirement has become the principal battleground in IRS examinations and litigation, and it is the requirement most often ignored by promoters. In Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37, the Tax Court disallowed a flour miller's credits for every claimed project because the taxpayer recited the steps of its technical work but did not document a methodical process of experimentation. In Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), the Seventh Circuit affirmed the disallowance of a shipbuilder's credits because the taxpayer failed to prove, with evidence rather than oral testimony alone, that 80% or more of its activities for each vessel constituted elements of a process of experimentation, while clarifying how direct supervision and direct support enter the "substantially all" fraction. These decisions show why a claim built from generic narratives cannot survive scrutiny, however confidently it is marketed.

Furthermore, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c) exclude several categories of activities even when technical personnel are involved. Excluded activities include research after the beginning of commercial production (§ 41(d)(4)(A); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)), which encompasses activities conducted after a business component is developed to the point where it meets its basic functional and economic requirements or is ready for commercial sale or use, such as preproduction planning for a finished business component, tooling-up for production, trial production runs, troubleshooting involving detecting faults in production equipment or processes, accumulating data relating to production processes, and debugging flaws in a business component. Also excluded are the adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need (§ 41(d)(4)(B)), the duplication of an existing business component from a physical examination, plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information (§ 41(d)(4)(C)), and surveys, studies, and certain other activities, namely efficiency surveys, management functions or techniques, market research, testing, or development, routine data collection, and routine or ordinary testing or inspection for quality control (§ 41(d)(4)(D); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5)). Internal-use software, meaning software developed for use in general and administrative functions such as financial management, human resources, and support services, is excluded under § 41(d)(4)(E) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6) unless it satisfies an additional three-part high threshold of innovation test requiring that the software be innovative, that its development involve significant economic risk, and that it not be commercially available for use by the taxpayer. Finally, foreign research conducted outside the United States, Puerto Rico, or any U.S. possession (§ 41(d)(4)(F)), research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities (§ 41(d)(4)(G)), and funded research (§ 41(d)(4)(H); 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)), meaning research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person, including situations where the taxpayer's payment is not contingent on success or where it retains no substantial rights in the results, are ineligible.

The funded-research exclusion is a recurring source of inflated claims by contract engineering, software, and architectural firms whose customer agreements shift financial risk or transfer all rights in the work product. Recent litigation illustrates the point: in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 979 (8th Cir. 2024), the Eighth Circuit affirmed that a structural engineering firm's research was funded where its contracts did not make payment contingent on the success of the research; in Perficient, Inc. v. Commissioner (U.S. Tax Court), the court addressed substantial-rights provisions that transferred documentation to customers; and in Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50 (June 16, 2026), the Tax Court analyzed the funded-research exclusion for an architectural partnership's projects and rejected a challenge to the validity of the long-standing funded-research regulations. A promoter who never reads the customer contracts cannot responsibly claim contract-based research.

items: "The Commission Hunter" (Percentage-Based Predatory Pricing): Charging contingency success fees of 20% to 30% of the tax benefit (with 25% cited in documented U.S. advisory examples), which establishes a linear financial incentive for the promoter to inflate QREs and push claims into high-audit-risk territory.

"The Kitchen Sink" (Scope Creep into Routine Business Operations): Disregarding the uncertainty and process-of-experimentation requirements under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) by reclassifying routine manufacturing adjustments, production maintenance, troubleshooting, or standard software updates as eligible process development.

"The Phantom Project" (Outright Fabrication of Documentation): Using generic templates or unverified generative AI outputs to fabricate technical narratives for R&D projects that never occurred or lacked any scientific basis.

body.text: The "Phantom Project" archetype collides directly with the IRS's heightened documentation requirements for research credit refund claims. Since its October 2021 Chief Counsel guidance (memorandum 20214101F) and subsequent transition guidance, the IRS has required a research credit refund claim to identify each business component, the research activities performed, the individuals who performed them, and the information each sought to discover, together with the total wage, supply, and contract research expenses. The IRS also revised Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) to add Section G business-component reporting, initially optional for tax year 2024 and phased in thereafter subject to exceptions for certain smaller claimants. Invented project narratives that cannot be tied to named employees, dated technical records, and general-ledger costs are therefore far more likely to be rejected at the claim-review stage or to collapse on examination.

Empirical enforcement data from the United Kingdom's HMRC underscores the scale of these abuses when unregulated "specialist" promoters target corporate claimants. In its 2022 to 2023 Annual Report and Accounts (published July 17, 2023), HMRC revised its estimate of error and fraud in UK R&D tax reliefs for 2020–2021 to 16.7% of the value claimed (£1.13 billion), up from a prior estimate of 3.6% (£336 million). After intensified compliance checks, a mandatory Additional Information Form for claims from August 8, 2023, and pre-notification requirements, HMRC's subsequent reporting estimated the overall rate at 7.8% for 2023–2024, with cumulative losses to error and fraud of more than £4 billion from 2020–2021 through 2023–2024. HMRC's random enquiry program found that roughly half of Small and Medium-sized Enterprise (SME) claims were at least partly non-compliant, and UK consultancy ForrestBrown reports that around 30% were found wholly non-compliant, with problems concentrated in small claims and in sectors where R&D is atypical, such as hospitality, arts, entertainment, and recreation. In extreme instances of "Phantom Project" fabrication, criminal prosecution follows: ForrestBrown reports that in the Convergica fraud case, a perpetrator claimed approximately £29.5 million in R&D tax relief against a fabricated £137 million of expenditure purportedly spent developing an IT healthcare system. These figures are UK data and do not describe IRS findings, but they illustrate the scale that promoter-driven claiming can reach when unchecked.
The Financialization of Tax Risk, IRS "Dirty Dozen" Warnings, and Non-Delegable Taxpayer Liability

The systemic driver connecting these practices is the financialization of tax risk. Predatory R&D promoters, and, according to TaxOps, even aggressive sales units within large accounting firms, entice executives with promises to double or triple their R&D credit estimates, or cold-call businesses in non-traditional industries while avoiding any discussion of audit downside. As noted by TaxOps, many aggressive vendors have operated on the assumption that historically low IRS staffing and declining audit rates minimize the likelihood that an inflated claim will be examined. That assumption ignores the extended limitations periods discussed below and the IRS's growing use of data-driven claim screening.

The IRS consistently flags aggressive credit promoters and misleading eligibility claims in its annual "Dirty Dozen" awareness campaign and official fraud guidance. Its 2025 and 2026 Dirty Dozen campaigns (the 2026 list was released in early March 2026 alongside National Slam the Scam Day), together with the IRS's Recognize Tax Scams and Fraud guidance, warn businesses and individuals against unscrupulous promoters, bogus credits and inflated refunds, misleading tax advice spread through social media, and "ghost" tax preparers, meaning paid preparers who refuse to sign the return or include their Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN), leaving the taxpayer legally responsible for errors or fraud. This pattern of promoter abuse has spanned improper Employee Retention Credit (ERC) claims, bogus "Self-Employment Tax Credit" promotions, false Fuel Tax Credit claims on Form 4136, improper sick and family leave credit claims on Form 7202, and fabricated undistributed long-term capital gains claims on Form 2439. The same playbook (cold outreach, percentage fees, and claims prepared without regard to eligibility) is the hallmark of an R&D credit scam.

When an aggressive R&D tax credit claim is challenged, the asymmetry between the promoter's reward and the taxpayer's liability becomes stark: the consultant has already been paid a percentage of the claimed benefit, while the corporate taxpayer bears non-delegable legal responsibility for the accuracy of its tax return. Relying on perceived low audit rates also fails to account for extended statutory look-back windows when carelessness, substantial omissions, undisclosed reportable transactions, or fraud are present. In the United States, the standard federal period for assessing tax is 3 years after the return is filed under 26 U.S.C. § 6501(a); the period extends to 6 years for substantial omissions of gross income exceeding 25% under 26 U.S.C. § 6501(e)(1); it remains open until at least 1 year after the required information is furnished where a taxpayer fails to disclose a Listed Transaction under 26 U.S.C. § 6501(c)(10); and there is no limitations period ("at any time") for a false or fraudulent return filed with the intent to evade tax under 26 U.S.C. § 6501(c)(1) and 26 CFR § 301.6501(c)-1(a). TaxOps notes that IRS reviews of aggressive claims frequently reach back seven years or more. In addition, because a disallowed credit carryforward can be adjusted in a later open year, an inflated credit generated in an otherwise closed year can still be reduced when it is used. In the United Kingdom, by comparison, under Paragraph 46 of Schedule 18 to the Finance Act 1998, HMRC's ordinary Corporation Tax assessment time limit is 4 years from the end of the accounting period (Paragraph 46(1)), extending to 6 years where a loss of tax was brought about carelessly by the company or a related person (Paragraph 46(2)), and to 20 years where a loss of tax was brought about deliberately (Paragraph 46(2A)).
UK 100% Inaccuracy Penalties vs. US Statutory Penalty Tiers

In the United Kingdom, as described in BDO UK's analysis and the statutory text of Schedule 24 to the Finance Act 2007, HMRC evaluates penalties whenever an R&D claim is found to be overstated, whether the error is discovered during an HMRC enquiry or disclosed through a voluntary amendment. Under Paragraphs 1, 3, 4, and 10 of Schedule 24, penalties are calculated as a percentage of Potential Lost Revenue (PLR) (the additional tax due or the excessive repayment claimed) based on the taxpayer's behavior and whether disclosure was "unprompted" (made when the taxpayer had no reason to believe HMRC had discovered or was about to discover the inaccuracy) or "prompted." Where the company took reasonable care, for example by giving complete information to a competent advisor and checking the claim before submission, no penalty applies. For careless inaccuracies, the maximum penalty is 30% of PLR, reducible to as low as 0% for unprompted disclosure or 15% for prompted disclosure, and a careless-inaccuracy penalty may be suspended for up to 2 years under Paragraph 14. For deliberate but not concealed inaccuracies, the maximum is 70% of PLR, reducible to 20% unprompted or 35% prompted. For deliberate and concealed inaccuracies, the maximum is 100% of PLR, reducible to 30% unprompted or 50% prompted. Under Paragraph 19 of Schedule 24, where a company's deliberate inaccuracy is attributable to an officer (including a director, shadow director, manager, or secretary), HMRC may give notice requiring the officer to pay such portion of the penalty, up to 100%, as HMRC specifies.

In the United States, by contrast, an excessive or fraudulent R&D tax credit claim under the Internal Revenue Code triggers a tiered structure of civil penalties rather than a single PLR-based scale. First, under 26 U.S.C. § 6676(a) (Erroneous claim for refund or credit), if a claim for refund or credit with respect to income tax is made for an "excessive amount" (the amount by which the claimed amount exceeds the amount allowable), the claimant is liable for a penalty equal to 20 percent of the excessive amount, unless it is shown that the claim has a reasonable basis or, for claims filed after December 18, 2015, is due to reasonable cause. Section 6676 does not apply to any portion of the excessive amount that is subject to the accuracy-related or fraud penalties. Second, under 26 U.S.C. § 6662(a)–(d) and (h)–(i) (Accuracy-related penalty on underpayments), the IRS imposes a 20 percent penalty on any portion of an underpayment attributable to negligence or disregard of rules or regulations, or to a substantial understatement of income tax. For a C corporation, a substantial understatement is one exceeding the lesser of 10% of the tax required to be shown (or, if greater, $10,000) or $10,000,000; for other taxpayers, it is one exceeding the greater of 10% of the tax required to be shown or $5,000. The rate increases to 40 percent for gross valuation misstatements (§ 6662(h)) and for nondisclosed noneconomic substance transactions (§ 6662(i)). Third, under 26 U.S.C. § 6662A(a) and (c) (Reportable transaction understatement penalty), an understatement attributable to a listed transaction, or to another reportable transaction (such as a transaction with contractual protection) a significant purpose of which is federal income tax avoidance or evasion, carries a 20 percent penalty, increasing to 30 percent if the transaction was not adequately disclosed on Form 8886. Fourth, under 26 U.S.C. § 6663(a)–(b) (Imposition of fraud penalty), if any part of an underpayment is due to fraud, a 75 percent penalty applies to the portion attributable to fraud; once the IRS establishes by clear and convincing evidence that any portion is due to fraud, the entire underpayment is treated as attributable to fraud except to the extent the taxpayer establishes by a preponderance of the evidence that a portion is not.

Crucially, in the United States, merely hiring a tax consultant or a large accounting firm does not automatically establish a "reasonable cause and good faith" defense under 26 U.S.C. § 6664(c) and 26 CFR § 1.6664-4. Under 26 CFR § 1.6664-4(c), reliance on professional advice is not reasonable if the taxpayer failed to disclose all relevant facts to the advisor, or if the advice was based on unreasonable factual or legal assumptions, such as blanket 100% wage allocations that the company's officers knew, or had reason to know, were unlikely to be true. Reliance is also unreasonable where the taxpayer knew or should have known that the advisor lacked knowledge of the relevant tax law, a significant risk when the "advisor" is an unlicensed sales organization. Moreover, under 26 CFR § 1.6664-4(d) and the Form 8886 instructions, a failure to disclose a reportable transaction is a strong indication that the taxpayer did not act in good faith, and for reportable transaction understatements 26 U.S.C. § 6664(d) makes adequate disclosure a precondition to any reasonable cause defense.
The Critical Risk of Contingency Fee Models and Regulatory Prohibitions

A primary structural indicator distinguishing predatory R&D credit promoters from compliant tax practitioners is the promoter's reliance on a contingency fee model. The fee model matters not only as a warning sign of misaligned incentives, but because the fee terms themselves can change the taxpayer's legal disclosure obligations.
The Perverse Incentive of Contingent Compensation and Circular 230 Restrictions

Under a contingency fee arrangement, frequently marketed to businesses as a "no win, no fee" or "success fee" structure, the consultant charges a fixed percentage of the gross R&D tax credit or refund identified. Industry analyses from Financial Solution Advisors indicate that R&D consultants working on contingency typically charge between 10% and 30% of the claimed recovery, with 25% of the R&D recovery cited as a common promoter fee in U.S. advisory literature. Because the consultant's revenue scales linearly with the size of the claimed credit while the taxpayer bears the post-filing audit and penalty exposure, contingent compensation creates a direct financial conflict of interest that rewards aggressive QRE inflation over conservative substantiation.

Recognizing that contingent fees compromise the objectivity of tax reporting, the U.S. Department of the Treasury restricts contingent fees in Circular 230 (31 CFR Part 10), which governs the practice of attorneys, Certified Public Accountants (CPAs), Enrolled Agents, and other practitioners before the IRS. Under 31 CFR § 10.27(a) and (b)(1) (as amended by T.D. 9359, effective for fee arrangements entered into after March 26, 2008), a practitioner may not charge an unconscionable fee in connection with any matter before the IRS and, except as provided in paragraphs (b)(2), (3), and (4), "may not charge a contingent fee for services rendered in connection with any matter before the Internal Revenue Service." Under 31 CFR § 10.27(c)(2), a "matter before the Internal Revenue Service" is defined to include tax planning and advice, preparing or filing (or assisting in preparing or filing) returns or claims for refund or credit, and all matters connected with a presentation to the IRS.

The enforceability of that rule, however, is now substantially narrower than its text. In Ridgely v. Lew, No. 1:12-cv-00565 (D.D.C. July 16, 2014), the district court, relying on the D.C. Circuit's holding in Loving v. IRS, 742 F.3d 1013 (D.C. Cir. 2014), that the preparation of returns is not "practice" before the IRS, ruled that the IRS lacks statutory authority to promulgate or enforce the § 10.27 contingent-fee restrictions with respect to the preparation and filing of ordinary refund claims (claims filed after the original return but before an examination), and it enjoined enforcement to that extent. The IRS did not appeal. Because R&D credits are very often claimed retroactively on amended returns or refund claims, the practical effect is that Circular 230 does not, by itself, prevent a practitioner from charging a contingent fee to prepare such a claim. Under the reasoning of Loving, Circular 230's reach over original-return preparation is also doubtful. Treasury and the IRS acknowledged these decisions in proposed regulations released December 20, 2024 (REG-116610-20), which would remove § 10.27 from Circular 230 entirely; as proposed regulations, they do not yet change the published text. Taxpayers should therefore not assume that a contingent-fee quote from a licensed professional is unlawful under Circular 230, nor that a licensed professional is barred from offering one.

Other rules remain fully in force. State boards of accountancy and the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct, ET § 1.510 (Contingent Fees), prohibit a CPA from preparing an original or amended tax return or a claim for a tax refund for a contingent fee, subject to narrow exceptions (for example, representation in an examination, or amended returns and refund claims based on a tax issue that is the subject of a test case or on which the taxing authority has developed a position). Most importantly, the reportable transaction rules discussed in the next section apply to the taxpayer whenever a fee is contingent or refundable, regardless of whether the advisor is a CPA, an attorney, an Enrolled Agent, or an unregulated marketing firm. Where § 10.27 can still apply, a practitioner governed by Circular 230 may charge a contingent fee only in four circumstances under 31 CFR § 10.27(b)(2)–(4):

items: Services rendered in connection with the IRS's examination of, or challenge to, an original tax return (§ 10.27(b)(2)(i));

Services rendered in connection with the IRS's examination of, or challenge to, an amended return or claim for refund or credit, provided the amended return or claim was filed within 120 days of the taxpayer receiving a written notice of the examination of, or a written challenge to, the original tax return (§ 10.27(b)(2)(ii));
Services rendered in connection with a claim for credit or refund filed solely in connection with the determination of statutory interest or penalties assessed by the IRS (§ 10.27(b)(3)); or
Services rendered in connection with any judicial proceeding arising under the Internal Revenue Code (§ 10.27(b)(4)).

body.text: Furthermore, 31 CFR § 10.27(c)(1) defines a "contingent fee" broadly to include not only a fee based on a percentage of the refund reported on a return or of the taxes saved, but also any fee arrangement in which the practitioner will reimburse the client for all or a portion of the client's fee if a position taken on a return or other filing is challenged by the IRS or is not sustained, whether through an indemnity agreement, a guarantee, rescission rights, or any other arrangement with a similar effect. Because unregulated boutique R&D consultants and marketing promoters operate outside the professional licensing rules governing CPAs, attorneys, and Enrolled Agents, they routinely market percentage-based fees, audit guarantees, or fee-refund promises. Whether or not those offers violate any professional rule, they create the reportable transaction exposure described below, which falls on the claiming company.
"Transactions with Contractual Protection," Form 8886 Disclosure, and IRC Section 6707A Penalties

Entering into a contingent-fee or fee-refund contract with an R&D promoter does not merely signal compromised due diligence. Under federal tax shelter regulations, the fee structure itself can make the R&D tax credit claim a reportable transaction carrying severe, independent statutory penalties.

Under 26 U.S.C. § 6011 and 26 CFR § 1.6011-4(a)–(b) (applicable to transactions entered into on or after August 3, 2007), every taxpayer that has participated in a reportable transaction must file a disclosure statement with the IRS. The regulations establish five categories of reportable transactions: listed transactions, confidential transactions, transactions with contractual protection, loss transactions under IRC § 165, and transactions of interest. Under 26 CFR § 1.6011-4(b)(4)(i)–(ii) and the Instructions for Form 8886, a transaction with contractual protection is any transaction for which the taxpayer (or a related party within the meaning of IRC § 267(b) or § 707(b)) has the right to a full or partial refund of fees if all or part of the intended tax consequences from the transaction are not sustained, or for which fees are contingent on the taxpayer's realization of tax benefits from the transaction. The rule applies to fees paid to any person who makes or provides an oral or written statement to the taxpayer, or for whose benefit a statement is made, as to the potential tax consequences that may result from the transaction.

In determining whether a fee is refundable or contingent, 26 CFR § 1.6011-4(b)(4)(i) directs that all facts and circumstances be considered, including the right to reimbursement of amounts the parties do not designate as fees, and agreements to provide services without reasonable compensation. Hourly or fixed fees therefore do not escape the rule if they are subject to a refund right or are payable only if the credit is realized. Under 26 CFR § 1.6011-4(b)(4)(iii)(B), a narrow exception applies where a person makes a statement regarding tax consequences only after the taxpayer has entered into the transaction and reported its consequences on a filed return, provided that person has not previously received fees relating to the transaction.

As highlighted in tax advisory analysis by CohnReznick and in the text of Revenue Procedure 2007-20 (2007-7 I.R.B. 517), the IRS used its exclusion authority to provide that refundable or contingent fees tied to eight specified credits are not taken into account under the contractual protection rule: the work opportunity credit (26 U.S.C. § 51), the welfare-to-work credit (26 U.S.C. § 51A), the Indian employment credit (26 U.S.C. § 45A(a)), the low-income housing credit (26 U.S.C. § 42(a)), the new markets tax credit (26 U.S.C. § 45D(a)), the empowerment zone employment credit (26 U.S.C. § 1396(a)), the renewal community employment credit (26 U.S.C. § 1400H), and the employee retention credit for employers affected by Hurricane Katrina, Rita, or Wilma (26 U.S.C. § 1400R(a), (b), or (c)). The Credit for Increasing Research Activities under 26 U.S.C. § 41 is not among the excepted credits.

Consequently, when a taxpayer claims an IRC § 41 R&D credit under a contingent-fee or refundable-fee agreement and does not meet the narrow post-reporting exception of 26 CFR § 1.6011-4(b)(4)(iii)(B), the arrangement triggers dual federal reporting obligations. First, under 26 CFR § 1.6011-4(d)–(e) and the Instructions for Form 8886, the taxpayer must attach a completed Form 8886 (Reportable Transaction Disclosure Statement), identifying the transaction as one with contractual protection, to its federal income tax return (including an amended return or application for tentative refund) for each tax year in which it participates in the transaction, and for the first year of participation must also send a copy of the Form 8886 to the IRS Office of Tax Shelter Analysis (OTSA), by mail or by fax (844-253-2553), at the same time. Because the IRS has updated the OTSA mailing address in the current instructions, taxpayers should confirm the address on IRS.gov at the time of filing. Second, under 26 U.S.C. §§ 6111–6112, a consultant who is a material advisor (generally, a person who provides material aid, assistance, or advice with respect to the transaction and receives gross income above the regulatory thresholds, which for non-listed reportable transactions are $50,000 where substantially all of the tax benefits go to natural persons and $250,000 in all other cases) must independently disclose the transaction on Form 8918 (Material Advisor Disclosure Statement) and maintain a list of advisees for inspection by the IRS. A material advisor who fails to comply faces penalties under 26 U.S.C. § 6707 of $50,000 for a non-listed reportable transaction or, for a listed transaction, the greater of $200,000 or 50% of the gross income derived from the transaction (75% for intentional failures), together with list-maintenance penalties under 26 U.S.C. § 6708.
Statutory Penalty Caps Under 26 U.S.C. § 6707A ($50,000 vs. $200,000)

body.text: As confirmed by the IRS Large Business and International (LB&I) practice unit on IRC § 6707A, the non-disclosure penalty for a transaction with contractual protection is capped at $50,000 per failure for a corporation, partnership, or other entity and $10,000 per failure for an individual, whereas the $200,000 entity and $100,000 individual caps apply only to listed transactions. 26 U.S.C. § 6707A(e) imposes a separate requirement that a company required to file reports with the Securities and Exchange Commission disclose certain § 6707A, § 6662A, and § 6662(h) penalties in those reports, with failure to do so treated as a failure to which the § 6707A penalty applies, but it does not change the per-failure caps in § 6707A(b).

The § 6707A penalty nonetheless remains exceptionally punitive. It is assessed without regard to whether the underlying credit was correct, there is no general reasonable cause or good faith defense, and it applies when a taxpayer that participates in a contingent-fee R&D claim fails to attach Form 8886 to its return, fails to send the required copy to OTSA, or files an incomplete Form 8886 (for example, one stating "information provided upon request"). The only statutory relief is the Commissioner's discretionary rescission authority under 26 U.S.C. § 6707A(d), which is limited to non-listed reportable transactions and to cases where rescission would promote compliance and effective tax administration, using the procedures in Rev. Proc. 2007-21; a rescission determination is not subject to judicial review. The IRS must also obtain written supervisory approval of the initial penalty determination under IRC § 6751(b)(1). Under 26 U.S.C. § 6707A(f) and 26 CFR § 301.6707A-1, the § 6707A penalty is imposed in addition to any other penalty, and the $10,000 / $50,000 limits apply separately to each failure to disclose, so participation across several tax years with no disclosure produces several penalties.
Hypothetical Worked Example: Step-by-Step Computation of Compounding Penalties on a Contingent-Fee R&D Claim
To illustrate how substantive and procedural penalties interact in practice, consider the following hypothetical corporate scenario, computed strictly from statutory rates:

items: Hypothetical Facts and Promoter Commission: Corporation X (a C corporation) engages an unregulated R&D tax consultant under a "no win, no fee" contingency agreement charging 25% of the claimed R&D credit. By improperly including sales and marketing wages ("technical sales") and routine production maintenance ("The Kitchen Sink"), the promoter inflates Corporation X's federal research credit on Form 6765 to $100,000, which Corporation X uses in full to reduce its income tax for the year, and the promoter collects a $25,000 contingent fee ($100,000 × 25% = $25,000). Corporation X does not attach Form 8886 to its return or send a copy to OTSA. On examination, the IRS determines that only $40,000 of the credit is substantiated by qualified research and disallows $60,000 ($100,000 − $40,000 = $60,000) as excessive.

Step 1: Repayment of the Disallowed Credit. Corporation X owes the $60,000 of tax that the disallowed credit had offset, plus statutory underpayment interest under 26 U.S.C. § 6601 running from the original due date of the return.

Step 2: IRC § 6707A Penalty for Failure to File Form 8886. Because the 25% contingent fee makes the R&D credit claim a transaction with contractual protection under 26 CFR § 1.6011-4(b)(4), Corporation X was required to disclose the transaction on Form 8886. Under 26 U.S.C. § 6707A(b)(1), the base penalty is 75% of the decrease in tax shown on the return as a result of the transaction (75% × $100,000 = $75,000). Because a transaction with contractual protection is a non-listed reportable transaction, 26 U.S.C. § 6707A(b)(2)(B) caps the penalty for an entity at $50,000 (the lesser of $75,000 and $50,000). Corporation X could request discretionary rescission under § 6707A(d), but cannot rely on obtaining it. (If the claim had instead been a listed transaction, where the entity cap is $200,000, the full $75,000 would apply; for a $300,000 listed-transaction tax decrease, 75% equals $225,000, which would be capped at $200,000.)

Step 3: Substantive Penalty on the $60,000 Disallowed Credit. In addition to the $50,000 § 6707A penalty, the IRS asserts one substantive penalty on the $60,000 underpayment, depending on the culpability finding. The substantive penalties are coordinated rather than stacked on the same dollars: § 6662 does not apply to any portion of an underpayment on which the § 6663 fraud penalty is imposed, § 6662A coordinates with § 6662 so that the same understatement is not penalized twice, and § 6676 does not apply to any portion subject to the accuracy-related or fraud penalties. Under Scenario A (20% negligence or substantial understatement penalty under 26 U.S.C. § 6662(a), or, where the credit was claimed on a refund claim and § 6662 does not apply, the 20% erroneous claim penalty under 26 U.S.C. § 6676(a)), the penalty is 20% × $60,000 = $12,000. Under Scenario B (30% nondisclosed reportable transaction understatement penalty under 26 U.S.C. § 6662A(c), which applies only if the IRS establishes that a significant purpose of the transaction was federal income tax avoidance or evasion), the penalty is 30% × $60,000 = $18,000. Under Scenario C (75% civil fraud penalty under 26 U.S.C. § 6663(a), if the overstatement involved fabricated "Phantom Projects"), the penalty is 75% × $60,000 = $45,000.

Step 4: Total Financial Fallout. Under Scenario A, Corporation X faces $60,000 (tax repayment) + $50,000 (§ 6707A penalty) + $12,000 (§ 6662 or § 6676 penalty) = $122,000 in IRS assessments, before interest. Adding the $25,000 paid to the promoter produces $147,000 of cash outflows to secure a legitimate credit worth only $40,000, a net loss of $107,000 before interest and audit defense fees. Under Scenario C (civil fraud), IRS assessments reach $155,000 ($60,000 + $50,000 + $45,000), and total cash outflows including the promoter fee reach $180,000, with the additional risk that the limitations period never closes under § 6501(c)(1) and that the matter is referred for criminal investigation. (By comparison, in the United Kingdom under Schedule 24 to the Finance Act 2007, £60,000 of PLR arising from a £100,000 claim would carry a maximum penalty of £18,000 [30%] for careless behavior, £42,000 [70%] for deliberate behavior, and £60,000 [100%] for deliberate and concealed behavior, before reductions for disclosure.)

body.text: Institutional Antithesis: Risk-Managed Compliance and Structural Integrity
Risk Governance, ISO Standards, and Multi-Jurisdictional Regulatory Alignment

ISO 31000 provides risk management guidelines and, as the International Organization for Standardization itself states, is not intended for certification. ISO/IEC 27001 is a certifiable standard, so any reliance on ISO/IEC 27001 certification should be confirmed against the issuing certification body's register.

Conservative compliance requires respecting the enforcement mandate of program regulators, such as the IRS in the United States and the dual-agency regulators in Australia, and establishing contemporaneous documentation before filing a claim. In Australia, as reflected in official guidance from the ATO and business.gov.au, the R&D Tax Incentive (R&DTI) is jointly administered by the Department of Industry, Science and Resources (DISR) through AusIndustry, which registers core and supporting R&D activities and assesses whether they meet the legislative criteria (including that the outcome could not be known or determined in advance on the basis of current knowledge, information, or experience), and by the ATO, which reviews expenditure and entitlement to the offset. Under ATO record-keeping guidance (records generally must be kept for 5 years), claimants must maintain contemporaneous time records for R&D salaries, apportion overheads on a reasonable basis, and comply with the program's statutory integrity provisions. These include the rule in section 355-480 of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 (ITAA 1997) that expenditure incurred to an associate can be claimed as a notional deduction only when it is actually paid; the "expenditure not at risk" integrity rule in ITAA 1997 section 355-405, explained in Taxation Ruling TR 2021/5, which denies notional deductions where the entity or an associate receives or could reasonably be expected to receive consideration as a direct or indirect result of incurring the expenditure regardless of the results of the R&D activities; and the arrangements flagged in ATO Taxpayer Alert TA 2023/4, Research and development activities delivered by associated entities (released December 14, 2023), which warns against arrangements in which an R&D entity incorrectly claims the offset for expenditure incurred under agreements with associated entities that conduct and benefit from the activities, exposing participants and promoters to increased scrutiny, penalties, and, where applicable, the promoter penalty regime in Division 290 of Schedule 1 to the Taxation Administration Act 1953 and the Part IVA general anti-avoidance rule.
Ethical Fee Alignment, Financial Independence, and the "No Benefit, No Fee" Regulatory Nuance

items: Time Billing (Hourly Consulting Approach): Billed at published hourly rates that "currently" range from $195 to $395 per hour depending on the professional involved and the actual time expended (for example, 2 hours at $395 per hour = $790 for an independent third-party review of a self-prepared software claim or for preparing a response to an ATO or AusIndustry request for further information).

Fixed-Fee Engagements: A firm, upfront fixed-fee quote provided after a complimentary scoping discussion and based on estimated hours, technical complexity, and project scope. Note, however, that the advisor's fee arrangement does not determine whether the taxpayer's own research is "funded" under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), which turns on the taxpayer's contracts with its customers or grantors.

Phased or Hybrid Engagements: A structured fee combining scheduled hourly rates and fixed-fee milestones (such as scoping, technical writing, and financial calculation), with out-of-pocket disbursements not charged unless an unforeseen, substantial cost is agreed in advance.

body.text: Technical Regulatory Analysis: The "No Benefit, No Fee" Fixed-Fee Provision

Under 26 CFR § 1.6011-4(b)(4)(i), a fee is contingent if it depends on the taxpayer's realization of tax benefits, and a fee is refundable if the taxpayer may recover it when the intended tax consequences are not sustained; the facts-and-circumstances test looks through labels, so a "fixed" fee that is payable only if a credit results, or that is sized by reference to the benefit, can be a contingent fee for reportable transaction purposes. The broader definition in 31 CFR § 10.27(c)(1) and CohnReznick's regulatory analysis point in the same direction. If a paid engagement letter makes the fee contingent on the taxpayer realizing the federal income tax credit, or refundable if the credit is disallowed, the taxpayer should analyze and, where required, make the Form 8886 disclosure under 26 CFR § 1.6011-4(b)(4). A free, non-binding eligibility assessment before any engagement is executed does not itself create contractual protection. For U.S. taxpayers seeking to avoid contractual protection triggers entirely, any fixed-fee or hourly engagement letter executed after initial scoping should be unconditional: the fee is owed for the professional time and substantiation work performed, without any refund or contingency tied to whether a credit is realized or sustained by the IRS.
The Multi-Disciplinary "Six-Eye Review" and Audit Defense Ecosystem

items: First Set of Eyes: The Qualified Engineer (Technical Eligibility and Project Boundaries). A qualified engineer evaluates candidate projects against the statutory IRC § 41 Four-Part Test (permitted purpose, technological in nature, elimination of uncertainty, and process of experimentation). The engineer filters out routine operations, post-commercial-production debugging, and non-technical roles such as sales and marketing, and works with the accounting reviewer to classify physical items correctly. That classification matters because supply QREs exclude property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation: in TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009), the Tax Court held that production molds the taxpayer sold to its customers were not depreciable in the taxpayer's hands and could therefore qualify as supplies used in the conduct of qualified research, a taxpayer-favorable result that turned entirely on careful factual classification of who owned and depreciated the tooling.

Second Set of Eyes: The Scientist (Experimental Methodology and Narrative Rigor). The scientist verifies that contemporaneous documentation (laboratory notes, iterative test logs, failed prototypes) substantiates a systematic process of experimentation meeting the 80% "substantially all" threshold for each business component, rejecting "result-only" narratives of the kind that failed in Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37, and Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023).

Third Set of Eyes: The CPA or Enrolled Agent (Financial Quantification and Tax Law Compliance). A Certified Public Accountant or IRS Enrolled Agent (or a Chartered Accountant in Commonwealth jurisdictions) conducts financial vetting. This specialist reconciles QRE allocations to the general ledger and Form W-2 Box 1 payroll records, removes ineligible G&A and overhead expenses, and reviews third-party contracts for funded-research and substantial-rights provisions under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d) to prevent contract-research disallowances of the type litigated in Perficient, Inc. v. Commissioner (U.S. Tax Court), Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 979 (8th Cir. 2024), and Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50.

body.text: Formal audit representation and any audit defense insurance coverage (described as covering CPA, tax attorney, and specialist consultant fees during an examination) are governed by the explicit terms of the client's written engagement agreement, or billed at the published $195 to $395 hourly rates for standalone controversy representation. Taxpayers should read any "audit defense included" promise with care: a guarantee to refund fees if a credit is not sustained is itself a contractual protection feature under 26 CFR § 1.6011-4(b)(4), whereas a commitment to provide representation services for an agreed fee is not.
Comparative Matrix: Predatory Contingency Promoters vs. Risk-Managed Compliance Standard

cells: Primary Financial Incentive
Claim Maximization: Revenue scales directly with gross credit size, incentivizing QRE inflation and rapid "quick kill" filings.
Risk Mitigation and Defensibility: Revenue is decoupled from credit size; prioritizes claims designed to withstand IRS, HMRC, or ATO examination.

Contingent fees create a conflict of interest. Circular 230 § 10.27 restricts them on paper, but after Ridgely v. Lew (D.D.C. 2014) it cannot be enforced for ordinary refund claims, and proposed regulations (REG-116610-20, Dec. 2024) would remove § 10.27. AICPA ET § 1.510 and state rules still bar CPAs from contingent-fee return and refund-claim preparation.
Fee Structure and Pricing
Contingency / Commission ("No Win, No Fee"): Typically 10% to 30% (e.g., 25%) of the claimed R&D benefit, or refundable fee guarantees.

Fixed Fee or Hourly Billing: Published hourly rates of $195 to $395 per hour, milestone hybrid fees, or scope-based fixed fees after free initial scoping; note the published fixed-fee option describes fees as a function of the benefit received.
Only unconditional fixed or hourly fees avoid contractual protection under 26 CFR § 1.6011-4(b)(4); a benefit-dependent "no benefit, no fee" term is a contingent fee for reporting purposes.
Wage and Activity Substantiation

"Kitchen Sink" and "Phantom Project" Inflation: Blanket 100% inclusion of sales and marketing ("technical sales") and G&A or accounting wages; routine maintenance or AI-fabricated projects claimed as R&D.
Contemporaneous Four-Part Test Substantiation: Strict separation of direct performance, first-line supervision, and direct support; contemporaneous time records and trial evidence.

Governed by 26 U.S.C. § 41(b) and (d), 26 CFR §§ 1.41-2 and 1.41-4, the IRS refund-claim specificity requirements and Form 6765 Section G, and (for Australia) ITAA 1997 ss 355-405 and 355-480 and ATO Taxpayer Alert TA 2023/4. See Siemer Milling (T.C. Memo. 2019-37) and Little Sandy Coal (7th Cir. 2023).
Reportable Transaction Exposure (Form 8886)
High Exposure: Contingent or refundable fees create transaction with contractual protection status; promoters routinely fail to advise filing Form 8886 (or to file Form 8918 themselves).
Low Exposure When Fees Are Unconditional: Structured to avoid conflicted fee triggers; independent of CPA assurance conflicts.

IRC § 41 is not among the eight credits excepted by Rev. Proc. 2007-20. The non-disclosure penalty under 26 U.S.C. § 6707A(b) is 75% of the tax decrease, capped at $50,000 per failure for entities ($10,000 for individuals) for non-listed contractual protection transactions; the $200,000 cap applies only to listed transactions. Discretionary rescission is available for non-listed transactions under § 6707A(d).
Substantive Audit and Penalty Risk

Severe Taxpayer Liability: Full clawback of the disallowed credit plus 20% to 75% US civil penalties (or, in the UK, up to 100% of PLR), plus extended look-back windows (up to 20 years in the UK; unlimited for fraud in the US).
Proactive Audit Readiness: Claims built as if already under examination; pre-filing mock audits via creditARMOR and audit defense terms defined in the written engagement agreement.

The UK 100% PLR cap (and officer liability) applies under Sch. 24 Finance Act 2007. US penalties are 20% (§§ 6662, 6676), 20% to 30% (§ 6662A), 40% (§ 6662(h)–(i)), and 75% civil fraud (§ 6663), coordinated so that the same dollars are not penalized twice.
Internal Quality Control and Staffing
Sales-Driven or Unregulated Preparers: Staffed by commissioned salespeople or generalist preparers using shortcut estimates without technical vetting.
Described "Six-Eye Review": Three-stage sign-off by a qualified engineer, a scientist, and a CPA or Enrolled Agent (including human review of TaxTrex AI output).

Provides multi-disciplinary review of technical eligibility (engineer), scientific method (scientist), and financial and tax compliance (CPA or EA), addressing the failure points seen in Siemer Milling, Little Sandy Coal, and the funded-research cases.
Governance and Standards
No Formal Risk Framework: Operates outside professional ethical standards, or relies on firm size (the "Big Four" illusion of safety) while billing high hourly rates for subsequent audit defense.
ISO-Aligned Risk and Security Governance: Framework aligned to ISO 31000:2009 (risk management guidelines) and ISO/IEC 27001 (information security), plus a reported BBB A+ rating.
ISO 31000 is not a certification standard (current edition ISO 31000:2018); ISO/IEC 27001 certification status should be confirmed with the certifying body.
